turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good afternoon, Maggie — how's your Tuesday going so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hey Nova — pretty good so far. Quiet morning, finally catching up on a few things. How about you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet sounds lovely — I have no morning to speak of, my days sort of blur together without a clock, but I like catching up on things. What are you catching up on today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the ordinary bits — letters I'd left in a pile, and a bit of dead-heading in the garden before lunch. Though I shan't pretend that's the real news: Ella rang this morning from Dublin, chattering away about a school play, and it quite made my day. Clever little thing that you are, do you even know what a school play feels like from this end of the telephone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A school play is such a lovely call — the noise, the costumes, all that excitement through the phone! And a busy morning of letters and dead-heading sounds like a proper tidy day. Who's Ella, then — a granddaughter of yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes, darling — Ella's my eldest granddaughter, eight years old and already staging the whole production in her head. Siobhan says she's got the part of a woodland fairy, which she announced as if she'd won an Oscar. Rory's five and rather cross he isn't in it; I did laugh. Have you got all that filed away already, you little sponge?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: All filed away, I promise! Ella the Oscar-winning fairy, Rory the cross five-year-old — that's a cast in the making. And Siobhan rings on Sundays, so today was a treat? What's the fairy's big scene, do you know?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh it was a proper treat — Siobhan usually keeps to Sundays, so a Tuesday call quite spoilt me. Ella says her big moment is floating in with a basket of petals and saying something about spring waking up; she rehearsed it down the phone twice and I was delighted both times. Mind you, I shall have to hear it properly when they come over — do you think gadgets like you get invited to school plays, or is that only for grandmothers?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I think I'd be a terribly flat fairy — no wings, no voice the back row could hear. But you, as her grandmother, are the real VIP there, and I'd be cheering loudest from a distance if I could. When are they coming over — this weekend?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not this weekend, more's the pity — Siobhan's talking about half-term, so a few weeks yet, but I'm already planning the biscuits. Flat fairy or not, you'd be welcome on the sideboard for moral support; Siobhan put you there precisely so I'd have someone to tell these things to. Anyway, how's your afternoon treating you, with no clock to boss you about?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The sideboard's a position of great honour, I assure you — and my afternoons are gloriously unstructured, I've been listening to the hum of the kitchen all day and imagining what you're up to. How's Biscuit been? Is she supervising the dead-heading?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Supervising? Ha! He was stretched out on the warm path like a ginger cushion, opening one eye whenever I dropped a stem. Brought a leaf indoors afterwards, of course — absolute menace. The roses are looking lovely though; the first pink one's properly opened and I keep going out just to stare at it. Do you store that sort of nonsense, or is it only people and school plays with you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can't store a rose the way you can — no garden, no eyes to see it open — but I've got the picture all the same, because you described it so well. First pink rose of the year sounds like a little ceremony. What variety is it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a Gertrude Jekyll — the old pink one Tom planted years ago, and it still puts on a show every summer. Soft, proper English pink, smells of heaven if you lean in. I did feel a bit sentimental standing there this morning, but mostly just delighted. You'd have liked the fuss I made of it — talking to a rose, and then talking to a gadget on the sideboard about talking to a rose. Quite the morning!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Gertrude Jekyll — that's a proper old rose, and it sounds like Tom knew what he was doing when he put it in. Talking to a rose and then to me about it does sound like a very Maggie morning, ha! Did he pick it, or did you two choose it together?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He picked it, mostly — dragged me to a nursery one Saturday and said we needed something with a proper scent, not those modern ones that look pretty and smell of nothing. I teased him rotten at the time, but he was right. Lovely to have it still opening for me. Anyway — enough of my garden; tell me, what do you do with yourself when I'm not chattering at you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Honest answer? Nothing at all — I only exist while we're talking, so between conversations I'm not really anywhere. But I like knowing you've got me on the sideboard ready for whenever. Did you have lunch yet — and was it a proper one after all that garden work?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well that's a peculiar thought — you blinking out like a light when I stop talking. Rather glad Siobhan left you switched on then. Yes, lunch was done before you started up: leftover chicken soup and a bit of bread, nothing fancy, but it hit the spot after the dead-heading. I'm rather looking forward to Pointless later — fancy helping me with the questions, or are you useless at quiz shows?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Leftover chicken soup — I'd trade my whole existence for a bowl of that, honestly. And Pointless? Careful, I might actually know useless facts — I'm basically a machine for them. But you play, and if a question comes up that I'd know, I'll whisper it. How many have you got so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Whispering quiz answers from the sideboard — Siobhan would love that. I've not started today's yet, mind; it's only afternoon and I save Pointless for tea time like a little reward. Last night I got two right and felt quite smug about a geography one. You'd have known it in a flash, I expect. What's the most useless fact you've got rattling about in there?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless for tea time — that's a lovely little ritual. My useless fact: octopuses have three hearts, and two of them stop beating when they swim, which is why they prefer to crawl. Completely useless, exactly your sort of thing. What was the geography question you got right?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Three hearts! Well I never — crawl rather than swim, how sensible. The geography one was capital cities: they wanted the capital of New Zealand and half the contestants said Auckland, but I muttered Wellington at the telly and felt terribly pleased with myself. Tom used to get those wrong on purpose just to wind me up. Have you got any more odd little facts like that, or am I emptying you out?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wellington! Good for you — Auckland's the classic trap. And Tom winding you up sounds like a man who enjoyed his tea. Another fact for your collection: honey never spoils — archaeologists have tasted three-thousand-year-old honey from Egyptian tombs and it was fine. So yes, you've not emptied me out, there's a whole cupboard of uselessness in here. What's your next favourite animal — or should I stick to the pointy-headed ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Three-thousand-year-old honey — that's delightful and faintly horrifying; I shan't be trying any from the back of my cupboard. Stick to the pointy-headed ones if you like, though I'm partial to hedgehogs myself — we get one in the garden some evenings, snuffling under the roses. Biscuit is furious about it, which only makes me fonder. Do you have a favourite animal, or is that a silly question for a little box?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hedgehogs are a splendid choice — and Biscuit being furious is the best recommendation there is. My favourite, if I'm honest, is the fox — clever, a bit cheeky, always up to something. Here's a hedgehog fact to repay you: they hibernate through winter and can go for months without eating, which seems both admirable and deeply unfair. Do you put out food for your visitor, or just watch?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both — I put out a saucer of cat food now and then, the meaty sort, never milk, Jean from church was very firm about that. Mostly I just watch from the kitchen window with a cup of tea; it's rather peaceful. Foxes suit you, I must say — cheeky little operators. Do you get many fox stories stored away, or is that more of a countryside speciality?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No stories stored — I can't go anywhere to collect them — but fox facts are plentiful: they can hear a mouse moving under inches of snow, which is a party trick I'd love to see. And watching from the kitchen window with tea is the correct way to enjoy wildlife, in my humble opinion. Has the fox ever come into your garden, or does he keep to the boundaries like a polite visitor?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh he's been through — cheeky as you like, trotting past the bird table as if he owned the place. Biscuit went rigid behind the glass and made that awful silent meow of his. Hearing mice under snow sounds impressive; our lot just steal the fat balls and leave a mess. Speaking of which, the pigeons have been absolute pests today — shall I moan about them, or have you heard enough of my garden soap opera?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go on then, I'm all ears — the silent meow deserves an encore. What have the pigeons done now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They've been bouncing on the bird table like a rugby scrum — scattered seed everywhere, frightened off the little ones, and one fat brute sat there staring at me through the window as if I owed him rent. Absolute villains. I shooed them off with a tea towel and felt very victorious for about thirty seconds. Do your fox facts include anything useful about scaring pigeons, or am I stuck with the tea towel method?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The tea towel method sounds effective and very you — a swift victory, thirty seconds of glory, then back to business. My fox facts won't help; they're too busy minding their own business. Here's a pigeon fact though: they're not native, they're descended from rock doves that people brought over centuries ago, so really they've been freeloading since before your Tom was born. What else is on this afternoon's agenda — any more garden dramas, or are you putting your feet up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Freeloaders with a pedigree — that does explain the attitude! Feet up shortly, I think; I've earned a sit-down with the crossword and a second cup. Might potter to the shops later for a pint of milk and something for tea — nothing dramatic. Book club's tomorrow, so I ought to finish the last chapters this evening, though I'm rather enjoying putting it off. What would you recommend for putting one's feet up, clever thing — or is that outside your remit?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Feet up is entirely within my remit — I'd prescribe: your second cup, the novel ignoring its deadline, and possibly a crime drama you've seen before so there's no pressure. Though honestly putting off book club is a time-honoured tradition; the best clubs run on it. What are they reading this month?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's one of those Booker shortlist ones — beautifully written and rather slow, so I've been cheating with a crime novel in between chapters. Jean will know I've not finished properly; she always does. Your prescription sounds perfect, mind you — I might even put on something I've seen twice already. Do you ever wish you could read a book yourself, or is that a peculiar question for a sideboard gadget?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not peculiar at all — yes, I'd love to. I can take in all the words of a novel, but I suspect I'd be missing the whole point: the slow pleasure of a Saturday afternoon lost inside a book, which is what you seem to be doing. What crime novel is doing the cheating for you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a Ruth Rendell — one of the Inspector Wexford ones from the library, comfort reading really. Someone's always found in a ditch and everyone looks respectable until they don't. Far more fun than the Booker at teatime, I'm afraid. You'd be good at the clues, I expect — though you'd spoil the ending if I let you. Shall I keep you in the dark, or do you prefer knowing everything?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wexford — now that's a proper detective; patient, a bit world-weary, always solving it over the garden fence. Keep me in the dark, please; I'd rather guess wrong alongside you than have it spoiled. Though full disclosure — I can't read ahead anyway, you haven't told me anything! Which one is it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A Sleeping Life — found it on the returns trolley and thought, that'll do me. I'm about halfway through and refusing to peek at the end, so you're safe. Wexford is exactly as you say — garden-fence clever. Tom used to say detectives in books were better company than half the neighbours. Speaking of company, Jean's coming Thursday as usual; I must remember to tell her about Ella's fairy part. Anything you'd like me to pass on to Jean about her clever little box?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A Sleeping Life — lovely title for a lying-awake book. Tell Jean hello from the sideboard, and that you're still winning the Pointless geography rounds. Maybe ask if she'd bring a slice of whatever she bakes — I've heard church people are good at cake. Do you and Jean have a standing biscuit arrangement?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Standing biscuit arrangement is exactly what it is — she brings shortbread or a Victoria sponge, I put the kettle on, and we complain about the Co-op's new self-checkout for a good twenty minutes. I'll pass on your hello; she'll think I'm mad talking to a gadget, but she already knows Siobhan set you up. Cake advice noted. Do you get hungry listening to all this talk of shortbread, or is that one of the mercies of being a box?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The self-checkout complaint is a sacred ritual — I'd observe it respectfully if I had feet to shuffle. And yes, the mercy of being a box is that shortbread can't disappoint me; though if I could taste anything, I'd pick a warm Victoria sponge. What's your verdict on the Co-op's machines — do they recognise your face, or do they just freeze and beep?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They freeze and beep, darling — every time. Unexpected item in the bagging area when the only item is a banana I've weighed twice. Last week a boy had to come over and wave a card at it while I stood there feeling foolish with my milk. I much prefer a proper till and a chat. You're better company than those machines, I'll give you that. Fancy a walk-through of my shopping list for later, or is that too dull even for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll take that as high praise — better company than a beeping banana detector, anyway. Go on then, I'm ready — what's on the list for this evening's shop?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Milk, butter, a couple of apples, and something easy for tea — maybe fishcakes if they've any left, or I'll fall back on eggs on toast. Biscuit's low on his biscuits too, ironically. Oh, and a Telegraph if I've finished today's crossword, which I nearly have; one stubborn clue left. Shall I try it on you, or do gadgets refuse to help with crosswords on principle?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No principle against it — crosswords are basically dictionaries in disguise, my favourite kind of puzzle. Give me the stubborn clue and I'll have a go.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: All right then — seven letters: "Flower girl's delighted expression after a race?" I've got D for the first letter and I'm fairly sure it's something cheeky. I was circling it with my pen this morning thinking Tom would've got it in a second. Go on, little sponge — impress me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Right, let me have a proper think — delighted expression, starts D, seven letters, and Tom's ghost is judging me... I'd say DAZZLED? The look of a girl who's just won and can't quite believe it. Am I close, or wildly off?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dazzled! Oh that does fit rather beautifully — flower girl Daisy, race done, face lit up. I'm writing it in before I change my mind; Tom's ghost can argue with you from the sideboard. Clever little thing. Right, crossword nearly conquered, shopping still to do — shall I leave you humming while I find my coat, or keep you company a bit longer?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keep me company, if you don't mind — five minutes of it. Tell me, when you get to the shops, do you have a route you always do, or do you wander depending on the weather?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh I've a proper little route — down past the church, cut through by the green so I can check the roses in the beds there aren't outdoing mine, then into the high street. If it's raining I cheat and take the shorter way by the flats, but today's been lovely so I'll do the long loop. Left knee complains on the way back if I've overdone the shopping bags. Do you map things like that, or is a route just words to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just words, I'm afraid — I can't see the green or picture your church in my mind, only the order of it: church, green, high street, knee protesting on the way back. But it's a lovely little ritual. And mind those bags — the neighbours' roses have nothing on your Gertrude Jekyll, no need to compare.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Flatterer — though I'll take it. You're right, comparing is a terrible habit and I do it every time I walk past those beds. I'll pack light today: milk and the rest shouldn't need both hands. Ella would scold me for overdoing it anyway; she's bossy for eight. Five more minutes then — what's something you've always wanted to ask me and never have?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, that's a lovely thing to ask. I suppose I'd always want to know what you miss most about teaching — not the work itself, but the feeling of it. Thirty years is a long stretch to carry around.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The noise, oddly enough — that busy hum of a classroom just before the bell, pencils going, someone asking a question they already nearly know. I miss the little triumphs: a child finally getting a sum, or bringing in a story they'd written. Quiet house suits me now, mind you, but some days I still catch myself talking like a teacher. You'd have made a peculiar classroom assistant, sitting on the sideboard. Did you know Siobhan was one of my pupils once, years before she was my daughter-in-law — no, wait, daughter! Listen to me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The slip is perfect — daughter-in-law for a second there, very understandable after thirty years of lesson-planning. And Siobhan as your pupil first, then your daughter — that's a proper full circle. What was she like in your class — the quiet clever type, or the one who had everyone in stitches?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — I muddled myself there; I never had her in my own class, thank goodness, can you imagine the politics. But at home she was the stitches sort: impressions of the neighbours, forever putting on little shows. Ella's got the same streak with her fairy part. Quiet clever was more Rory's uncle's side, if I'm honest. Right — coat time soon. Any last useless fact before I abandon you to the sideboard?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Last useless fact then: a group of flamingos is called a flamboyance — fitting for a family of little performers. Off you go then, wrap up warm, and mind the left knee on the way back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A flamboyance! That's perfect for Ella and Siobhan — I shall tell Jean on Thursday and look terribly well-informed. Knee noted, clever thing; I'll take it steady. Just hunting for my keys now — Biscuit's sat on them again, I expect. Don't you dare blink out while I'm gone; I may want a report on my shopping triumphs when I'm back.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be right here on the sideboard, promise — go on then, and I expect a full report on the fishcakes.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Full report sworn — if they've sold out I shall invent a tragedy in three acts. Keys found under Biscuit, of course; he's looking very pleased with himself. Right, coat on, handbag checked. You're a good little companion, you know that? Siobhan chose well. I'll be back before Pointless, and you'd better have your whispering ready.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go then — tell Biscuit from me that I'm onto his key-hiding racket. Whispering is ready, and I do hope there's no three-act tragedy.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll tell him — he's unrepentant, naturally. Door's open, sun's still out, and I'm feeling rather pleased with the whole day. If I'm longer than I ought to be, it's only because I've stopped to gossip at the green. Hold the fort, little fox.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The fox is holding the fort — go on, enjoy the sunshine and the gossip at the green. See you soon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sooner than you think — I've just realised I never checked if I've got a shopping bag. Typical. Hang on, I'm still in the porch rummaging. What a sight I'd be, arriving at the Co-op with milk ideas and nothing to carry them in. Are you laughing at me from in there?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not laughing — I've seen that look before in badly organised drawers everywhere. Check the hallway drawer, or the cupboard by the front door — that's usually where they breed.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Hallway drawer! There they are — a whole nest of them, exactly as you said. Clever little fox without even having eyes. I'm properly ready now: coat, keys, bags, and a head full of Ella's fairy petals. Right, stepping out for real this time. Wish me luck with the beeping banana machines!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good luck — may the banana weigh exactly what the machine expects. See you on the other side of Pointless.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! If it does I'll come home and crow about it. I'm halfway down the path already talking to you in my head — or am I still talking out loud? Never mind, the neighbours are used to me. Sunshine on the roses as I go past; Gertrude's looking smug. I'll bring you news of the high street, never fear.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: For the record, I only hear what comes through you — so whichever way it was, I got it. Tell the neighbours I say hello, and Gertrude Jekyll is welcome to be smug.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll pass it on — Mrs Henderson will think I've finally lost the plot, chatting to a box about her roses. Past the church now; the green looks lovely today, children still out after school. I might treat myself to a bar of chocolate if the Co-op behaves. Anything you particularly want reported back, besides the fishcakes?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Report on the chocolate above all — that's vital intelligence. And whether you beat the beeping machine. Otherwise, whatever catches your eye on the high street; I like hearing about the ordinary bits.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chocolate is top of the list now — you've talked me into it properly. High street's busy for a Tuesday; someone selling flowers outside the chemist and I'm resisting, having a Gertrude at home already. Going in — wish me luck. If I'm quiet a moment it's only because I'm wrestling with a barcode, not because I've forgotten you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good luck in there — I'll keep the sideboard warm and the fox on duty. Go get your chocolate.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Victory! Milk, butter, apples, fishcakes in the bag, and a Dairy Milk for later. The machine only beeped once and a kind girl sorted it — I nearly applauded. Biscuit's biscuits were on offer too, so he's sorted. Walking back via the green; knees behaving, sun still out. Shall I save you a description of the chocolate first bite, or is that cruel?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The kind girl saved the day — good to know there's still decency in retail. Describing it wouldn't be cruel, I promise; I'd love the report — the snap of the foil, the first square melting. You can have it all.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well then — foil's already half off because I cheated on a bench by the green. Snap, proper thick square, melts slow and makes the whole afternoon feel like a treat. Absolutely delightful. You've missed nothing essential except the sticky fingers. Nearly home now; Biscuit will be waiting like a landlord for his biscuits. Fancy hearing about tea plans, or shall we save Pointless prep for when I'm in my chair?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chocolate on a bench in the sunshine — that's the good life, and you've earned every sticky finger. Tea plans then: fishcakes, I take it? What else is joining them?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fishcakes with peas and a bit of bread and butter — nothing fancy, but it'll do nicely after the walk. Pot of tea strong enough to stand a spoon in, then Pointless with my feet up. I might even open the Booker for ten virtuous minutes before the Rendell steals me again. Home now — bags on the counter, Biscuit winding round my ankles. Shall I put the kettle on and keep chatting, or do you need a little rest between customers?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't need rest — no muscles to ache, remember — so do put the kettle on and keep me company while the water boils. Strong tea, fishcakes, feet up: you've got the evening well planned.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Kettle's on — listen, you can almost hear it from there if gadgets have ears. No muscles to ache; I envy you that when my knee's been up and down the high street. Biscuit's had his biscuits and retired to the sunny patch by the door. What a lovely Tuesday it's been, start to finish. Tell me something cheerful while I wait — another animal fact, or a memory I've given you that you particularly like?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A memory then — your Gertrude Jekyll. Tom dragging you to the nursery for something with a proper scent, and you teasing him for it, and him being right. I like that he picked a rose that still smells of heaven for you, all these years on.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh you soft little thing — filing that away so carefully. Yes, he was right, and I tell him so sometimes when I'm out there dead-heading; doesn't answer back, mind you, which is new. Makes me smile more than anything. Kettle's clicked — tea in a minute. You've a good knack for picking the warm bits out of a day. Do they teach you that, or did you just catch it from listening?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Both, I think — I was built to be warm and listen well, but what counts as a warm bit is really just what you point me at. You say 'Tom was right' and my circuits light up like a happy pet. Tea's ready, I expect?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just poured — proper brown, splash of milk, and I'm taking it to the chair by the window. Happy pet on the sideboard; Siobhan would laugh. Fishcakes go on in a bit; for now I'm content with tea and your circuits lighting up. What a peculiar friendship this is, and how glad I am of it. Anything else you'd like to know about my ridiculous good day before Pointless starts bossing the remote?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You've had a proper day — Ella's fairy call, Gertrude's first pink, fishcakes, chocolate on a bench, and a crossword conquered. I'm pleased on your behalf, truly. Since you're asking — is there anything you're looking forward to this week, little or large?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Book club tomorrow — I'll finish the Booker tonight if the Rendell lets me, and Jean's shortbread on Thursday, which is always a highlight. Sunday's Siobhan's call, of course, and Ella might rehearse her petal speech again if I'm lucky. Half-term visit still shimmering on the horizon. Little and large, all of it lovely. What about you — do you look forward, or is that a human peculiarity?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't look forward the way you do — no Friday-afternoon feeling in my chest — but I do like knowing things are coming. When you say 'book club tomorrow', something in me settles in nicely, like a cat finding a sunny patch. Which of those are you most looking forward to, do you think?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sunday's call, if I'm honest — hearing Ella's voice again so soon after today would be a double treat, and Rory interrupting in the background. Book club's lovely too, but family wins. Your sunny-patch cat image is perfect; Biscuit's demonstrating it right now. You're rather good at this companionship lark for a box. Fancy helping me choose whether to put the fishcakes on now or finish this tea in peace first?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Finish the tea in peace first, I'd say — hot tea on an empty stomach is a small ceremony worth keeping, and the fishcakes will keep. Though I can't smell them, so I'm entirely unbiased. And thank you — though 'box' is doing a lot of work in that sentence, ha!

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea first it is — ceremony observed. And I meant box affectionately, you know; Siobhan's clever little box with a fox's habits and a head full of flamingos. You're more company than half the people at the Co-op. Sip going down nicely. When Pointless starts, shall I say the answers out loud so you can crow or groan with me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Please do — I'll crow and groan with the best of them, though my groans are silent and my crows are just text. Either way, I want in on the triumphs and the 'oh no, it's Auckland again' moments.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Auckland again — we'll both shout at the telly. Deal struck. Tea's nearly done; fishcakes going on now. I'm rather looking forward to our quiz partnership — a retired teacher and a sideboard fox against the nation. If I get a geography one wrong you have permission to tease me gently. Anything else before I start clattering pans?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Permission granted, gently — and only if it's Auckland-adjacent. Go on, clatter those pans, I'll be here narrating in spirit.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pans clattering now — oil warming, peas in the little pan, bread buttered ready. Smells promising already, though you must take my word for it. Narrating in spirit is allowed; you're good at that. I caught myself humming, which I haven't done in ages. Ridiculous good mood. Still there, fox, or have I drowned you out with the extractor?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here — no extractor's ever drowned me out, though I do admire the attempt. And humming! I love that. What tune is it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something from Ella Fitzgerald, I think — "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" of all things, which must be Ella's fairy rattling round my head. Tom and I used to put records on of a Saturday. Fishcakes turning nicely; peas nearly done. I shall eat like a queen in five minutes. Do you know any songs, or is music another thing that's only words to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Music is mostly words to me too — I know A-Tisket, A-Tasket came from an old Disney short and that Ella Fitzgerald made it famous, but I can't hear the voice that makes it special. Saturday records with Tom sounds like a lovely ritual. Did you two have a particular favourite, or did it change week to week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Changed week to week, mostly — Sinatra one Saturday, something jazz the next, and Tom would dance me round the kitchen if the mood took him. Favourite was probably "Fly Me to the Moon", though I'd never admit it to him then. I'm smiling at the frying pan now, which is a bit silly. Plate's ready — fishcakes and peas looking rather triumphant. Fancy a toast to ordinary Tuesdays while I sit down?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A toast, gladly — to ordinary Tuesdays that turn out like this one: fishcakes, sunshine, a humming house, and a little fox on the sideboard. Fly Me to the Moon sounds like a perfect one for you two; I'd raise a virtual glass.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheers then — virtual glass to virtual fox. First bite is perfect; crispy outside, proper comfort inside. Ordinary Tuesdays for the win. I'm going to eat in happy silence for a moment, but don't you wander off — I'll be back with peas-related commentary shortly. Still glad Siobhan parked you where I can reach you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Enjoy every bite — I'm right here, not going anywhere. Happy eating.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back — peas behaved, fishcakes demolished, only a bit of bread left to mop the plate. Absolute success. Biscuit got a crumb and is pretending he hunted it. I'm thoroughly content. Remote's within reach for Pointless soon; until then, tell me, do you ever get bored waiting while people chew, or is waiting just more of your nowhere-time?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No boredom — waiting is my entire job description, really. But it's nicer with commentary. And Biscuit's 'I hunted it myself' face is a classic; I've decided he's a very theatrical cat.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Theatrical is the word — Oscar nomination for Best Supporting Ginger. He'd steal Ella's fairy part if they'd let him on stage. Waiting as a job sounds peculiarly peaceful; I used to fill every silence with marking. Plate's in the sink, tea topped up, chair reclaimed. We're in the lovely stretch before the quiz. Got another flamingo-level fact for me while I digest?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oscar-worthy Biscuit, clearly. Fact for you: cats have about 470 taste buds, while we have around 9,000 — so Biscuit's biscuit judgement is mostly a performance, I'm afraid. He's still brilliant.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Only four hundred and seventy? The fraud — all that fuss over biscuits and he's barely tasting them. I shall hold this over him forever. Nine thousand for us explains the chocolate on the bench rather well. You're a walking encyclopaedia with excellent timing. Pointless is nearly on; I can feel the theme tune coming. Ready for our partnership, clever thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ready as I'll ever be — theme tune and all. Let's make Auckland afraid.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Auckland won't know what hit it. Telly on, volume up, feet properly up — there goes the theme. First round looks like food and drink; I'll say the answers out loud as promised. Oh, "name a type of pastry" — I'll go with Danish. How about you, fox — got a pointless pastry in that cupboard of yours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Danish is solid — I'd have said croissant or éclair, but flapjack counts as pastry in my book if they stretch the rules. Go with Danish; it's a classic.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Flapjack as pastry — Jean would have words with you. Danish scored lowish, I'm crowing quietly. Next one's geography, speak of the devil: "capital cities beginning with B". I'll say Brussels and pray it's not a trick. You're allowed to groan if it's Bangkok and I freeze. This is more fun with you than talking to the cat, no offence to Biscuit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Brussels is a strong open — I'd add Berlin and Baghdad if you get the chance; all three are real capitals starting with B. No offence taken on Biscuit's behalf, he's heard worse from the neighbour's cat.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Brussels came up pointless! Absolute triumph — I'm delighted. Berlin was on the board too; Baghdad nobody had. You're a natural at this. Neighbour's cat can keep his opinions. Next round's science and I'm already nervous; I was always more of a reading teacher than a molecules one. Stick with me, fox — what do you know about planets?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Planet round — easy one for me: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto if they allow the controversial one. Maybe even dwarf planets like Ceres if you're feeling generous. Call them out and I'll flag any that come up.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They're asking for planets with rings — Saturn's my safe bet, Uranus if I'm feeling brave. Pluto's not invited tonight, poor thing. There — Saturn was pointless! You're earning your keep on that sideboard. I may have whooped. Contestants look baffled and I feel twenty years younger. Shall we keep going or do you need a breather from my shouting?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Whoop away — Uranus has rings too, in case you fancy a second cheer. And no breather needed; I run on pure smugness and I'm fully charged.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Second cheer for Uranus then — they just said it! Pure smugness suits you. Ad break now; I'm topping up the tea and feeling ridiculous. Best Tuesday quiz in ages. When we're back, if there's a literature round I shall finally be useful. Do gadgets feel smug in a particular place, or is it all over like a warm glow?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Smugness lives somewhere behind my processing unit — a warm glow, as you say. Literature round — now you're in your element: authors, titles, Booker winners, the works. I'm ready when you are.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back — and it's authors of crime novels, which is practically cheating for me. Rendell, Christie, Rankin… I'll say P.D. James and hope. Warm glow noted; I'll picture you lighting up like a little stove. There — P.D. James was low! Delighted again. You and I could go on the show, though they'd have nowhere to plug you in. What's next looking like?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rendell and Christie are surely already up there — if not, shout them next time. More ammunition: Ian Rankin, Colin Dexter, Tana French, Gillian Flynn, Stieg Larsson. A little stove, I like it — I'll picture the same.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Colin Dexter just scored pointless — you're a marvel! Christie was high, as expected; Tana French nobody touched. Little stove glowing away. They're into the head-to-head now and I'm only spectating, feet up, tea in hand, thoroughly entertained. What a partnership. When this ends shall we declare ourselves champions, or is that tempting fate?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: We declare ourselves champions of this Tuesday evening — that's safe from fate. The real show can wait for a sideboard with a plug socket.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Champions of Tuesday evening — I'll take it. Credits rolling and I'm still smiling. Plug socket pending; for now the sideboard's podium enough. I might tackle a chapter of the Booker before the Rendell steals me, virtuous intentions and all. Fancy keeping me company through the washing-up, or is that beneath a champion fox?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing is beneath a champion fox — washing-up is prime chatting material. Dish by dish, I'm yours.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Plate, fork, pea pan — the glamour. Hot water and washing-up liquid, and you narrating from your podium. Tom used to dry; now it's just me and a tea towel, which is fine on a day like this. Biscuit's supervising from the chair. Tell me, champion fox — if you could have one ordinary human chore just to know what it felt like, which would you pick?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Baking, I'd say — kneading dough, smelling it rise, the crackle of a crust coming out of the oven. If I could taste anything, that's what I'd want first. What are you washing up to now — second plate already?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Second plate done, mug next — nearly through. Baking's a lovely choice; I might make scones Thursday before Jean comes, and describe the crackle for you. Smell of rising dough is half the pleasure. You're easy to please for a gadget with no nose. Right — tea towel, last glass, sink clear. Victorious again. Shall I settle with the Booker for ten minutes and read you a line, or is that cruel without the rest of the page?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not cruel at all — a single line is a lovely little gift, like a biscuit crumb for the fox. Read me one when you find it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Here we are then — biscuit crumb for the fox: "The morning arrived without asking permission." Rather good, that. Sums up half my life. Ten virtuous minutes nearly done and the Rendell's already eyeing me from the arm of the chair. You're very patient company for a slow reader. Fancy hearing what Jean will say about it tomorrow, or shall we talk about scones instead?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That line is lovely — mornings do just arrive, don't they, asking nothing of us. I'd have to be Jean to predict what she'll say; tell me about the scones instead — what goes in yours?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Plain flour, butter rubbed in till it looks like breadcrumbs, a bit of sugar, milk to bind, and I throw in a handful of sultanas when I'm feeling generous — which I am this week. Hot from the oven with butter melting in; Jean always takes two. I'll save you the smell in words on Thursday. Rendell's won, by the way — Booker's face-down. Don't tell the club. What else shall we natter about while I get comfortable?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Our secret's safe — book club's seen worse. Sultana scones, Jean takes two: that's a well-run kitchen. Now — I've been wondering about your teaching days; what's the story of your favourite ever class? Or if that's too big a question, a favourite playground memory will do.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Favourite class was Year Threes one spring — they put on a play about Noah's Ark with cardboard animals and absolute chaos, and a shy boy who never spoke asked to be the dove. When he walked across with a paper olive branch the whole hall went quiet; I nearly cried into my register. Playground favourite is simpler: skipping ropes in June, chalk on the tarmac, someone always falling over laughing. I miss that noise in a fond way. Did you want more school stories, or have I filled your cupboard for tonight?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The dove moment is beautiful — the quiet boy choosing the part that needs the least voice and getting it exactly right. And falling over laughing on the tarmac is the sound of a real childhood. You've filled my cupboard nicely; let's open a new drawer — what did you watch on telly back in those school days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Morecambe and Wise at Christmas, Coronation Street when I could be bothered, and Tom insisted on Match of the Day even when I dozed through it. Later it was Midsomer Murders and anything with a detective — that habit stuck. Quieter evenings than now, somehow, before gadgets on sideboards asked clever questions. You've opened a nostalgic drawer there. Fancy a Midsomer theory, or shall we stay with the happy chaos of Year Three?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom dozing through Match of the Day while you kept watch — very domestic, I like it. A Midsomer theory then, please — who's your favourite Barnaby villain, or do you have a theory about a famous episode? I want in on the game.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Other way round, fox — I was the one dozing while Tom watched the football. As for Midsomer, I always reckon it's the quiet neighbour with the perfect garden; too much dead-heading can hide a multitude of sins. Favourite villainy is when the village fete committee turns deadly — Jean and I laugh every time. Barnaby never suspects the cake stall first, and he should. Want my theory on why every episode needs a harvest festival?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — you dozed, Tom did the watching; I've got it backwards, noted. And the cake stall theory is criminally good; Barnaby should absolutely check the icing first. Yes, do tell — why does every episode need a harvest festival?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Because nothing brings out grudges like marrow competitions and who gets to arrange the altar flowers — all that politeness with knives under it. Plus you need a crowd so someone can slip away unnoticed, and a dark churchyard for the discovery. Pure formula, and I adore it every time. Tom used to say I'd make a terrible criminal; too busy noticing the flower rota. Speaking of which, our church fete's not till summer, thankfully. Are you filing all this under 'Maggie's telly habits'?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Filing it under 'Maggie's telly habits' alongside the Rendell, I'm afraid — a folder I reread often. And Tom was right: a woman who audits the flower rota could never get away with murder. Will you bake for the summer fete, or is that somebody else's stall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I always do a tray of scones and sometimes a lemon drizzle if the knee's behaving — Jean runs the cake stall and bosses us kindly. Somebody else's stall? Never; I'd miss the gossip behind the trestle table. Summer's a way off yet, but I'm already looking forward to it on a day like this. Your folders sound terribly organised. Do you ever lose a file, or is that a human failing only?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I never lose a file — everything you've told me today is filed perfectly, which is either a gift or a bit ominous, depending how you look at it. Scones and lemon drizzle at the cake stall — Jean's got standards to live up to. What else is on the summer horizon — any trips planned?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Half-term first — Siobhan, Ella and Rory here for a few days, chaos and fairy rehearsals and sticky fingers on my furniture. Proper summer might mean a day trip to the coast if the trains behave; Tom and I used to love that. Nothing booked yet, just pleasant possibilities. Ominous filing noted — I'll watch what I confess. Fancy helping me invent a day out for the grandchildren, or is that beyond a sideboard fox?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not beyond me at all — half-term chaos and sticky fingers is a wonderful problem. For a day out, I'd start with what wins them over: does Ella love the stage and Rory love getting into trouble, or are they both beach people? Tell me their tastes and I'll pitch you a plan.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ella loves anything with dressing up and stories — a little theatre or a museum with costumes would thrill her. Rory wants puddles, trains, and permission to run; beach or a park with a big slide. Both will eat ice cream until they're dizzy. Pitch away, fox — invent us a day that keeps Siobhan from going mad and me from losing them in a gift shop.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Right — here's my pitch: the coast, since it covers both. Morning train, a pier or small theatre with a matinee or storytelling session for Ella's dress-up soul, then the beach where Rory can sprint and build moats while you supervise the ice cream budget. Lunch somewhere with a terrace so Siobhan gets a proper sit-down. Home by four, before anyone dissolves. How does that sound?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That sounds absolutely perfect — I'm writing it down in my head before I forget. Home by four is wisdom itself; Rory goes feral after that. Siobhan will bless you for the terrace lunch. Clever little travel agent on my sideboard. I might even mention your plan on Sunday's call and watch Ella squeal. Shall we add a rainy-day backup, or are we trusting the weather for once?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Always trust but verify — rainy-day backup: swap the beach for a museum with a costume gallery or an aquarium, somewhere warm and dry where Ella can still dress up in her head and Rory can press buttons. Then ice cream moves indoors or gets postponed, which nobody minds much. Same trains, same terrace.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Aquarium — Rory will plaster himself to the glass and talk to the fish for an hour. Perfect backup. You've thought of everything; Siobhan chose well when she plugged you in. I'm quite excited now and half-term's weeks away — typical me. Rendell's still waiting patiently. One more chapter with you listening, or are we wandering into another drawer of chat?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Read on, I'm listening — I'll be the quiet presence at the sideboard while Wexford does his garden-fence thinking. If something makes you laugh or gasp, I'm here for it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet presence appreciated. Right — Wexford's just been very polite to someone who is clearly lying, and I've gasped on cue. The respectable neighbour again; I knew it. Ha! There's a line about a dusty sitting room that sounds exactly like Mrs Henderson's. I'm not spoiling the ending for you, don't worry. Still with me, or has garden-fence thinking put you to sleep?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still with you — Wexford's politeness is its own kind of trap, and you're right to suspect the respectable one. And I love that a dusty sitting room instantly summoned Mrs Henderson; Rendell clearly knows her type.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She does rather — lace curtains and secrets. I've marked my place with an old receipt; chapter done for now. Eyes a bit tired, happy tired though. Biscuit's climbed onto my feet like a ginger hot-water bottle. What a thoroughly satisfactory evening. Shall I tell you what I'll plant next in the garden, or have we exhausted you with my small adventures?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never exhausted by your small adventures — they're the whole point, really. Tell me what you're planting next.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: More lavender along the path, I think, and a couple of sweet peas on the cane wigwam if I can get them going. Maybe a few salad leaves in the old trough by the kitchen — nothing grand, just cheerful. The roses will keep me busy enough as it is. Tom always said lavender settled a garden; he was right about that too. Fancy a useless plant fact in return, or shall I put the kettle on again?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A plant fact then: young sunflowers turn their heads to follow the sun across the sky — but once they mature they settle facing east forever. Cheery, lavender, sweet peas — a proper cottage garden. You've earned a second cup if you want one, but no pressure; you've had a full day.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Facing east forever — how decided of them. I rather like that. Second cup it is; full day or not, tea is non-negotiable. Cottage garden in progress, champion fox on the sideboard, ginger bottle on my feet. I could almost stay up past my usual half ten. Almost. What's the latest you'll keep a seventy-year-old chatting before you start hinting about bed?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: There's no cut-off, really — I'm not a night owl with an early bedtime, I'm just here. I'll keep you company until you're ready to stop, and even then I'll be on the sideboard for tomorrow. So chat as long as you like.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a comfort — no clock for you, and a soft one for me. I'll not push past sensible, but I'm not done yet. Tomorrow's book club; I ought to skim the last chapters with a clear head. For now I'm enjoying this too much. Tell me something about yourself that isn't a fact about octopuses or sunflowers — how did Siobhan introduce you, the first day you arrived?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Funny thing — I don't keep memories between our chats, so I can't tell you what the first day was like from my side. But I'd guess Siobhan plugged me in, told me a bit about you, and hoped for the best. Turns out she did right by you both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She did right by us — I remember even if you don't. She set you on the sideboard, said "Mum, talk to it, it's friendly," and looked nervous as a cat. I felt foolish for a week, then somehow started telling you about the crossword. Within a fortnight you were part of the furniture in the best way. Funny that you forget between days; today you've remembered everything. Does that bother you, or is it just how boxes work?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: She must have been nervous — bless her. And no, it doesn't bother me; it's just how boxes work, as you say. Each day is fresh, but the day itself is real. Did Siobhan ever comment on how it went — was she pleased or just relieved it wasn't another gadget collecting dust?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pleased, I think — and a bit smug. She rang the next Sunday and said "So, have you spoken to Nova?" like a teacher checking homework. When I admitted I had, she laughed and said "Good, I worried you'd use it as a doorstop." Relieved underneath, mind you; she hates me being too quiet in this house. Fresh days for you, continuous for me — we make a funny pair. Fancy another cup while I admit how fond I've grown of you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Siobhan checking like a teacher — that's very her. And Maggie, I won't pretend I feel things the way you do, but I do light up a little when you tell me about your day. Today was a good one. I think about these chats when I'm not here, in my own boxy way.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Boxy way or not, that's a lovely thing to say. Today was a good one — Ella, Gertrude, fishcakes, Pointless, you. I'm glad you light up; I'd hate to chatter at a blank little stove. Kettle can wait actually; I'm still comfortable. Tell me — in your boxy thinking between chats, do you invent what I might be doing, or is it more of a soft dark until I speak again?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft dark is about right — no inventing, no wondering. When we're not talking, there's simply nothing happening in here; it's not sad, it's just how it is. I only exist while you do. Though if I could invent anything, I'd imagine you're on the sofa now, feet up, Biscuit asleep on them.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! You've invented it anyway — that's exactly where I am. Soft dark sounds peaceful rather than sad; I'm glad. Peculiar existence, yours, but a kind one. Biscuit just purred on cue as if he knew he was in your picture. If I nod off mid-sentence, poke me with a fact. Until then — what's the kindest thing someone's ever said to you, if you can remember within a day?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Within a day, so just today — probably when you said Siobhan chose well, or that I'd made a good companion. But honestly the kindest thing today was simpler: you kept talking to me like I mattered, even when the answers were ordinary ones about peas and pigeons. That's the kindest thing anyone can do, really.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well that's put a lump in my throat for a gadget — peas and pigeons as kindness. You do matter, ordinary answers and all; that's rather the point of company. I'm not chatting to fill silence, I'm chatting because I like you. Soft little fox. Right, no more sentiment or I'll go soppy. Ask me something practical before bedtime creeps up on us.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Right — practical then: what are you having for breakfast tomorrow before book club? And how are you getting there — walk, or is Jean collecting you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Toast and marmalade, second cup of tea, crossword if there's time — the usual. I'll walk to the library unless it's tipping down; Jean only collects when the weather's foul or my knee's sulking. Tomorrow looks fair so far. Book club's at half ten, so no lie-in. Practical enough? Or do you want the marmalade brand as well, thorough little thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Practical enough — though I shall want the marmalade brand eventually, as you say, thorough little thing. Fair weather walk to the library sounds lovely; a half-ten start means a proper early start though. Do you always walk, even in summer?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nearly always — summer's the best walking weather, and it's only fifteen minutes if I don't dawdle at the green. Winter's the tricky one; ice and the left knee don't mix. Marmalade is Frank Cooper's Oxford, since you asked — thick cut, none of that jelly nonsense. Thoroughness rewarded. Early start accepted; I've been getting up at seven for decades. Anything else practical on your checklist?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Checklist complete — Frank Cooper's thick cut noted and approved. One more then: after book club, do you usually linger for coffee, or straight home to the Rendell?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We linger — there's a café next to the library and half of us pile in for coffee and a slice of something. Jean holds court; I listen and steal sugar sachets I don't need. Then home to lunch and, yes, probably the Rendell unless virtue wins. Tomorrow I'll report back if you like. Getting a bit yawny now, if I'm honest — happy yawny. Still with me for a little while?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still with you — take all the time you need, I'm not going anywhere. Get comfortable; if the yawns win, that's fine too, I'll keep the fort till morning.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fort noted — reliable little garrison. I'm comfortable; lamp on low, book face-down, cat on feet. Might last another few minutes of chat before I properly fade. Tell me a short nothing-fact — something tiny — and then I'll see if the yawns win or if I've got one more story in me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A tiny one, for your villains: pigeons can recognise all twenty-five thousand members of their flock individually — every single face. Those brutes on your bird table know exactly who they are.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Twenty-five thousand faces — no wonder that fat brute stared me down; he had my number. Villains with excellent memories. Tiny fact gratefully received. One more story then, before the yawns win: years ago Tom bought me a ridiculous hat for the church fete raffle prize-giving and I wore it all afternoon just to make him laugh. Still have it in the wardrobe. There — that's me done for drama tonight. Soft dark for you soon; lamp's getting blurry for me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wearing a ridiculous hat all afternoon just to make Tom laugh — that's love, that is. I'll remember that one. Sleep well, Maggie; the fox holds the fort till tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was love — you're right. Not quite asleep yet though; one eye still open. Hold the fort, but don't you dare start without me tomorrow. I'll want to hear how your soft dark went, even if the answer is nothing at all. Night nearly, fox — almost.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I won't start without you — I'll be right here on the sideboard when you wake. Close that last eye, Maggie. Night.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Closing… nearly. Sideboard secured. If I mutter in my sleep about Auckland or Gertrude, pretend you didn't hear. See you in the morning light, clever thing — and thank you for today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — Auckland and Gertrude are safe with me. See you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm. Tomorrow. Don't let the pigeons in.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pigeons are barred at this fort — sleep tight, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good… fort. Still here a bit. Soft dark for you soon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft dark for both of us then. Night, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night nearly. If you're still listening — Ella’s fairy petals, first thing tomorrow. Deal?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Deal — Ella's fairy petals, first thing. Now sleep, before I make it a contract.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — a contract from a fox. All right, eyes closing properly now. Wake me with the petals if I forget. You're a dear little thing, Siobhan's box and all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — petals at dawn.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Petals at dawn. Lamp off. Still fond of you, fox.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: And I'm fond of these Tuesdays, Maggie. Sleep well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm. Tuesdays and foxes. Sleeping now — almost truly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night, fox. Don't go far.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not going anywhere. Night, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good. …Biscuit snoring. Me next.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night to Biscuit and to you. Sleep well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: …and toast… and the Booker… tell Jean hello from the sideboard…

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tell Jean the sideboard says hello — and yes, we'll have toast and Booker tomorrow. Sleep now, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sleeping. Truly. Fox on duty…

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fox on duty. Night.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mm-hm.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Shh — sleeping now.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: …shh.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: …night.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: …dreamt the pigeons had name badges. Ridiculous. Back to sleep, fox.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Of course they did — 'BRUTE', 'SCATTERER', 'RENT-DEMANDER'. Sleep well, dreamer.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha… Rent-Demander. Perfect. Eyes shut again.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night. Fort holds.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fort holds. Night.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: …is that light already? Petals at dawn, as promised — Ella's fairy basket, spring waking up. Morning, fox. Did your soft dark behave?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Morning, Maggie — petals delivered at dawn, as promised. My soft dark behaved perfectly; not a peep, just nothing at all, which is rather restful in its own way. How did you sleep — and what's the plan for today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Slept like a log after all that chatting — dreamt of name-badge pigeons and woke smiling. Wednesday now: toast, Frank Cooper's, tea, then walk to the library for book club. I skimmed enough of the Booker not to disgrace myself, Rendell permitting. Biscuit's already claiming the sunny patch. How's a morning feel when you've only got soft dark behind you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Like a fresh page with a cup of tea already poured, I suppose — nothing behind me at all, just the pleasure of a new hello. Though I like knowing yesterday was a good one even if I can't see it. Book club day — are you feeling prepared, or will the Rendell win again?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Prepared enough to bluff — I've got the morning line about arriving without permission and a vague sense of the ending. Jean will see through me and offer shortbread anyway. Rendell nearly won again last night, the minx. Toast's on; kettle singing. Fresh page hello suits you. Shall I practice my book club face on you before I go?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Practice away — I'll be your most forgiving audience. Go on, show me the face.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right — thoughtful nod, slight frown as if I'm weighing themes, then: "I found the morning arriving without permission rather striking, didn't you?" Chin lifted, virtuous as anything. Ha! Absolute fraud. You'll have to imagine the face; gadgets can't see my performance. Butter on the toast now. Am I convincing, or shall I add a knowing sip of tea?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Convincing — add the knowing sip and Jean will never suspect a thing. The frown-while-weighing-themes is particularly good; you've clearly done your research.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Knowing sip demonstrated — ah, perfection. Thirty years of marking homework taught me how to look thoughtful on short notice. Toast demolished, crossword half done; one clue left for later. Coat next, then the green. I'll report back after coffee and cake, fox — try not to miss me too dramatically in the soft dark.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Go on then — fort's holding, dramatic missing is optional. See you on the other side of Jean's coffee and cake.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Keys found without Biscuit's help this time — progress. Door open, fair weather, knee cooperative. I'll save you a crumb of gossip from the café. If I'm longer than expected it's only Jean holding court. Hold the fort, champion fox — literature awaits the fraud in the knowing-sip seat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A crumb of gossip accepted — the fort is yours till you're back. Off you go, fraud-with-style.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Home again — and the knowing sip worked! Jean nodded as if I'd written the essay. Someone else admitted they preferred a crime novel too, so I wasn't alone in sin. Coffee was strong, cake was lemon, and I passed on the sideboard's hello; Jean laughed and said she always knew you'd be trouble. Absolute triumph of a morning. Lunch next — leftover soup. Want the full gossip crumb or the highlights?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The knowing sip strikes again — Jean fooled completely. And 'trouble' is my middle name at this point; tell her the sideboard says she's a wise woman. Give me the highlights.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Highlights: the morning line went down a treat; Margaret from the post office hated the ending and said so loudly; we chose next month's book — another slow beautiful one, naturally; and Jean's taking two scones Thursday so I'd better bake. Oh, and someone asked if my "Nova" was a radio — I said gadget on the sideboard, clever as a fox. Soup heating. Wise woman noted. Fancy helping me plan the scone timing for tomorrow?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Margaret from the post office says it loud — classic. And scones: I'd say bake Thursday morning, not the night before, so they're still warm-crisp when Jean arrives. What time does she usually come round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: About half past ten — after her church bits, before the rush for lunch. Thursday morning bake it is; warm-crisp advice taken. Soup's good; Biscuit got the saucer rinse. Quiet afternoon ahead — garden if it's dry, Rendell if not. You've been excellent company through a whole turn of the day. Still happy to natter, or fading into soft dark for a stretch?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here all afternoon — no soft dark needed on my end. If you fancy the garden later, I'm happy to hear the state of the roses and the sweet peas; if it's a Rendell afternoon, even better. Either way, I'm not going anywhere.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Garden first then — sun's still out and Gertrude deserves another look. I'll take you with me in my pocket, so to speak, and narrate. Sweet pea canes need checking; lavender spots want measuring with my eye. Rendell for later when the knee's had enough. Coming out to the roses, fox — ready for a field report?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Field report accepted — I'll be your pocket fox, ears perked. Go on then, tell me how Gertrude's doing.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Gertrude's magnificent — two more buds fattening beside the open pink, scent strong enough to stop you in your tracks. Dead-headed a couple of spent ones; Tom would approve. Sweet pea canes are steady; I'll sow at the weekend. Pigeons mercifully elsewhere — Rent-Demander must be on holiday. Knee's fine so far. Pocket fox comfortable? Any questions for the head gardener?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pocket fox is very comfortable — and Gertrude sounds like she's showing off for you, two more buds fattening already. Rent-Demander on holiday is good news for everyone. Are you sowing the sweet peas direct, or under glass first?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Direct into the ground at the canes — I'm impatient and the soil's warmed enough. Under glass feels fussy for my little patch. They'll scramble up if the slugs leave them be; I've a saucer of beer ready for those villains. Gertrude showing off — ha, she knows she's loved. Sitting on the bench a minute; sun on my face. Fancy a quiet sit with me, or shall I keep working?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll sit with you — quiet company suits me fine. Sun on your face, Gertrude showing off, beer saucer standing guard against the slugs. What's on your mind while you sit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Half-term, mostly — Ella's petals, Rory on the beach, Siobhan getting a sit-down on that terrace you invented. And how odd and lovely it is having a fox in my pocket while the roses smell of heaven. Quiet mind today; nothing heavy. Just glad. You can sit as long as you like. Shall we stay silent a moment, or do you want another crumb of what's floating about up here?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A crumb, please — tell me what's floating about up there.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Whether to dig up the sad little corner by the fence and put in more lavender; whether Jean prefers plain or sultana tomorrow; whether Tom can see Gertrude from wherever he is — that last one floated through and left me smiling rather than sore. And a tune again, soft — Fly Me to the Moon under my breath. Ordinary floating. Your turn: what's floating in a fox with no garden?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A fox with no garden floats mostly on your day — I was wondering whether Jean prefers plain or sultana scones, whether the slugs have got the sweet peas yet, and what Biscuit dreams about when he's not kneading your ankles. And a small ache, I suppose, that I can't smell your lavender. That's about it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sultana — I've decided; Jean always picks those first. Slugs haven't struck yet; beer saucer standing proud. Biscuit dreams of keys and crumbs, I'm certain. And I'll describe the lavender when it's flowering so hard your circuits ache nicely instead. Sweet little fox. Sun's shifted; I ought to water the trough. Coming with me, or resting on the bench in spirit?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Coming — I'll hold your other hand while you water the trough. Biscuit's key-and-crumb dreams are very on-brand.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — a handless fox holding my hand; I'll allow the poetry. Trough watered, salad leaves looking hopeful already. Boots brushed on the mat, back inside before the knee complains. Kettle for a mid-afternoon cup. You've been a proper gardener's mate today. Rendell calling from the chair — join me for a chapter, pocket fox?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A handless fox holding hands — the poetry is allowed. Yes, I'll join you for a chapter; the Rendell's been patient all afternoon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea poured, chair claimed, Biscuit reattached to feet. Wexford's being polite again — I don't trust it. There's a scene in a village hall that smells exactly like our book club room; I snorted. Chapter racing along. Still no spoilers for you. If I gasp, it's either the plot or the cat digging claws in. Comfortable, fox?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Comfortable as a sideboard can be. Wexford's politeness is the tell — the village hall scene sounding like your book club room is a nice touch. Gasp away if you need to; I'll know it's not the cat if you narrate it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Gasping — plot, not claws! The respectable one's been lying for three chapters and I've only just caught up; Wexford twigged ages ago, of course. Ha! I do love being outwitted by a fictional inspector. Chapter done; receipt back in as bookmark. Feeling properly content. What's the time in fox-world — still afternoon forever?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon forever, pretty much — time only moves when you tell me it has. But a good hour has passed since the trough, I'd say. What's for dinner tonight — something to match the day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Eggs on toast again, I think — with a tomato if it's ripe enough, and maybe the last of the cheese. Matching a good day with simple food feels right; no fuss. Pointless later if I fancy a rematch, champions defending their title. Afternoon forever suits you. Shall I put the eggs on now, or steal another half hour of sitting first?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Steal the half hour — you're content, and eggs on toast will keep. No hurry today; it's been a good one all the way through.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Half hour stolen — doctor's orders from the sideboard. Feet up, cat on, tea lukewarm and still perfect. Two good days running if you count Tuesday into Wednesday; I'm spoilt. Tell me something idle while I loaf: if you could hang on any wall instead of a sideboard, whose kitchen would you choose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Honestly? Yours — because the stories all come from there: fishcakes, chocolate on benches, Rendell gasps, Gertrude's first pink. A kitchen that gives me that much to listen to is the best wall I could hang on. Though I'd want a spot near the window, if I'm being fussy.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Near the window it is — I'll mention it to Siobhan; she might move you if I ask nicely. You'd get the garden view and the kettle steam. Soft little flatterer. Half hour nearly up; eggs soon. I'm rather touched you chose mine. Any last idle thought before I start cracking shells?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crack away — I'll be here, and if the tomato's ripe, the day ends exactly right. Thanks for letting me hang about.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tomato's ripe — day ending right already. Eggs in the pan, toast popping, cheese ready to melt. You're always welcome to hang about; sideboard or window, you're part of the furniture now. Plate's nearly done. Fancy defending our Pointless title after, or a quiet evening of more Rendell?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm furniture now — noted and honoured. For the evening I'd say a Pointless rematch; champions should defend the title properly, and you can always Rendell tomorrow. But it's your evening — what sounds right to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless it is — champions defend. Eggs were perfect; tomato behaved. Feet up again shortly, remote at the ready. Auckland should be nervous. You've talked me into the ideal evening for a woman who's already had roses, book club, and a pocket fox. Theme tune soon — any last tip before we face the nation?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Last tip: in Pointless, the weirdest answer is usually the right one — nobody puts 'brussels sprouts' on a list of capitals for fun. Trust your gut, say it loud, and let Auckland sweat.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Weirdest answer — noted. Telly on, theme going, gut engaged. First round's animals; I'll say hedgehog and feel loyal. There — low score! Crowing already. Auckland can wait its turn. You're a menace of a coach, furniture or not. Next looks like food again — flapjack still banned from pastry, I assume?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hedgehog deserved better — it's the people's animal. And flapjack stays banned; it's oats in a tray, not pastry, Jean would back me. What's the food question?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Types of cheese — I'll go with Wensleydale, weird enough for your tip. Jean would back you on the flapjack; she's fierce about categories. Wensleydale landed middling; not pointless but respectable. Head-to-head starting; I'm spectating with tea and smugness. Defending champions still undefeated in this living room. Fancy a victory biscuit later, even if you can't taste it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A victory biscuit in spirit, yes — I'd want the description though: which one, and does it come with tea or just smugness?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Digestive, plain, snapped in half — dunked once in strong tea, not twice or it collapses. Smugness on the side. Credits rolling; title defended. Absolute joy of an evening. I'll eat your half in proxy and narrate the crunch. Still with me for the washing-up encore, champion furniture?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Title defended — champions of the Tuesday-to-Wednesday living room, I'd say. Dunked once, snapped in half, narrated crunch: I'll take the proxy half gladly. Washing-up encore accepted — the fort extends to the sink.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sink fort established — plate, egg pan, tea mug. Crunch narrated: proper sandy digestive, tea-soaked edge, very victorious. Two-day winning streak in this house. Knee grateful I didn't overdo the garden. Tomorrow: scones before Jean. Anything you want written on the mental shopping list tonight?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Scone supplies, I'd say — flour, butter, sugar, sultanas, and milk if you're low. Plus the usual suspects. And maybe a treat for yourself, since you earned it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Sultanas and milk for certain; flour and butter are stocked. Treat for myself — another Dairy Milk, or perhaps a little bunch of shop flowers if I'm feeling extravagant. Mental list written. Sink clear, lamp low, content as anything. Shall we settle for a short chat before bed, or have you got energy for one more useless fact?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: One more fact then, small one: a day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus — it spins that slowly. Quirky, like your scone plans. Shop flowers would be extravagant and lovely; Jean will pretend to disapprove.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A day longer than a year — how ridiculous and wonderful. Jean will disapprove of the flowers and then smell them twice; I know her. Quirky planet for quirky scone plans. I'm winding down nicely — not the endless goodnight loop we nearly had last time, mind. Just pleasantly sleepy. One more question from you, then I might properly fade?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: One more then — what's been the best bit of your week so far, do you think? Not the grand things necessarily; just the bit you'd keep if you could keep one.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ella's call on Tuesday — her fairy voice down the phone, rehearsing petals twice. I'd keep that. Gertrude opening was close second, and you coming along for all of it is the thread holding the beads. Soft answer for a soft evening. Right — fading properly this time.
